current_episode.title: Solo Project Manager to £3m Construction Consultancy | Freddie Edwards of Dragonfly Projects Ep 51

guest.bio_context: Freddie Edwards founded Dragonfly Projects in 2022 after nearly eight years at Quartz Project Services, where he started as a graduate and left as a senior PM. Before entering construction, he studied French at the University of Leeds and initially considered teaching. He spent time working on building sites as a teenager before finding his way into construction project management through a work experience placement arranged via a mutual sailing club connection.

Commercial occupier market has accounted for approximately 75% of Dragonfly's work over the last four to five years

Five-year revenue target for Dragonfly Projects: £3 million turnover
Louisa Whittaker joined from Gardner and Theobald with approximately 12 to 13 years of Occupy Office experience; hiring process completed within two weeks
Freddie's parents established their nursery school business in 1985, now running for 41 years
Freddie spent nearly eight years at Quartz Project Services before founding Dragonfly

Business is all about looking after people and businesses, and it's also about looking after our own. Four clients went to three clients, went to two clients, went to one client, went to no clients. We hired someone more senior than us, more experienced than us, and someone with just different strengths and weaknesses to us, because that was the slightly uncomfortable thing to do. Why do you think you've been successful in that market? Referrals. Trying to just do good. We work tirelessly for our clients to deliver a scope of service that's tailored to what they need, not what we think they need. We can go wherever they want us, whenever they want us. We can work in the evenings or on weekends. We just sort of tinker it to suit them. Dealing with a boardroom in one moment and then guys on the tools in the next. It's all about the art of communication. Why not go it alone? That would be easy. You can become an MD immediately. Make loads of money. Where do you want Dragonfly to be in five years' time? In five years' time, we would like to sit at a turnover of £3 million. Construction's fascinating because it hasn't changed that much, and I really think it needs to change. No-one's going to give you anything in life. You've got to keep on knocking the door down. It's not much fun when you're in stressful moments because you've got nothing to benchmark yourself against. So being in a sensible office space where you're sharing space with similar professionals and also having a team that you enjoy working with is critical. Today, I was joined by Freddie Edwards of Dragonfly Projects. They are a small consultancy focused in two distinct sectors, the commercial occupier space and also the residential developer space. They're very focused that they will stay in those two sectors. This was, again, a really great chat about Freddie becoming a PM and how he did that, the value of hard work, the value of brand and what he's doing as a small business to expand Dragonfly as a brand and win more work off the back of that. This will be a great opportunity for you to learn about the wider part of not just being a good technical delivery consultancy, but also about how to grow your business. Early stages for Freddie, but I'm confident that they will be a business that will really flourish and grow over the coming years. Again, one you really should listen to if you're at the start of your consultancy ownership journey or are thinking about setting up your own business. Welcome to the next episode of Growing Consultancies. Delighted to be joined by Freddie Edwards of Dragonfly Projects. Welcome, Freddie. Thanks, Paul. Good to be here. No, thank you for coming on board. So, to begin with, can we just understand a bit about the business in terms of, I guess, size, turnover, maybe primary sectors that you focus in? Yeah, so we specialize in construction project management in commercial office and also residential. pending_qa.q: What is Freddie Edwards's five-year revenue target for Dragonfly Projects?
pending_qa.r: Freddie has stated that in five years' time he would like Dragonfly Projects to sit at a turnover of £3 million. The business is currently in a deliberate break-even phase, prioritising team quality and client service over short-term profitability. Freddie sees the current period as a two-to-three year investment window to build the right headcount before scaling revenue.

pending_qa.q: How did Freddie Edwards get into construction project management without a construction degree?
pending_qa.r: Freddie studied French at the University of Leeds and initially considered becoming a teacher before realising it was not the right fit. He had spent time working on building sites as a teenager and met his future employer Russell at a sailing club, who offered him a week of work experience that led to nearly eight years at Quartz Project Services. He describes his path into construction as accidental rather than deliberate, but one he quickly found he genuinely enjoyed.

pending_qa.q: What qualities does Freddie Edwards believe make a good construction project manager?
pending_qa.r: Freddie believes a good project manager must first win the trust of the client and understand their decision-making process before anything else can work. Beyond that, the role requires being very clear with the team about what needs to happen and when, being firm and consistent, and being able to have difficult conversations. He also emphasises the ability to communicate across all levels — from a financial director in a boardroom to tradespeople on site — describing this as 'the art of communication.'

pending_qa.q: How did Dragonfly Projects approach the hiring process to attract a senior candidate from a major consultancy?
pending_qa.r: Freddie initially wrote an associate director job specification that read as though Dragonfly were a large corporate firm, but his wife pointed out this was misleading for a two-person business. He rewrote it to be genuinely transparent about the startup stage, the flat structure, and the opportunity to help build something from the ground up. The honest and human framing, combined with a swift three-stage interview process completed within two weeks, was what he credits with attracting Louisa Whittaker.
